en: What it doesn't show: This does not mean every spooky coincidence in the real world is mere chance. The model assumes features are uniform and independent, which real features are not, so real matches may be more or less frequent. The birthday-problem probabilities only show that there are many possible pairs; they cannot tell whether a particular event was chance. And the fact that matches are common somewhere does not make it wrong to feel something special when it happens to you: the chance of matching me is low, so it is right that it feels rare. This page contains no statistics on real-world coincidences or how often they occur.

The birthday problem is a classic, well-known problem in probability. I understand the name "law of truly large numbers" comes from Diaconis & Mosteller (1989), "Methods for studying coincidences", Journal of the American Statistical Association 84. This project does not reproduce the numbers of that paper and shows the same idea with its own simplified model.

The calculated values are exact formulas. The chance that N people all differ on one feature is (1−1/c)(1−2/c)…(1−(N−1)/c), and since features are independent, the product gives "no matching pair in the room". The chance of matching me is 1 − Π(1−1/c)<sup>N−1</sup>. The dots are counted by actually running many gatherings (800 per point in ②, 400 in ③).

You can verify with node tools/validate-coincidence.js. For birthday only: 23 people give 50.7%, 57 people give 99.0%, and the smallest headcount where a match with me passes 50% is 254 (253 besides me).
The code is available on GitHub.
The Friendship Paradox · Simulatio Lab
Why do your friends tend to have more friends than you? Popular people show up on many friend lists. Build a network and click a person to check it yourself.

Look around and your friends seem to know more people than you do. It is tempting to blame your own social skills. But in a network like this, almost everyone sees the same thing. Change the number of people, how much popularity concentrates and the average number of friends to check.

People join one at a time. The first few are all friends with each other, and each newcomer befriends a few existing people (half the average number of friends), so the average number of friends stays near the slider value.

Who a newcomer befriends depends on hub concentration. At 0% anyone is picked with equal chance; at 100% people who already have more friends are more likely to be picked ("the popular get more popular").
For each person it computes my number of friends and the average number of friends my friends have, and compares them. If the friends' average is bigger, that person has "friends with more friends".
Press play and it repeatedly draws one random person (black ring) and one friend named by another random person (dashed gold ring), comparing the two averages.

What it shows: Across 300 different networks of 150 people with 6 friends on average and 80% hub concentration, a person had 5.92 friends on average, but their friends had 10.17 friends on average, 1.72 times as many. Computing "friends' average" for each person, 82.6% had friends with more friends (75.3% to 88.7% depending on the network), and 16.8% had more friends than their friends' average. The reason is that a popular person appears on every one of their friends' lists. In one network, the top 10% by friend count (15 people) held 29.6% of all friend-list slots. Picking a random person gave 5.92 friends on average, but picking a friend named by a random person gave 10.17. Even with 0% hub concentration, 71.3% had friends with more friends, and 85.4% at 100% (6 friends on average), so more concentration widened the gap. Connecting people at random did not make the result go away. It only needs people to differ in how many friends they have.

What it doesn't show: This does not mean that people with more friends are happier or that you are unpopular, and nothing here measures real friend counts or popularity. The network is this project's simplified construction: everyone has at least a few friends (no loners), and there are no real-world clusters like families, neighbourhoods or schools. What is guaranteed is the average (friends' average is at least the average friend count); that a majority has friends with more friends is a result of this model, not a law for every network. Hub concentration of 0% is not a fully random network but a "pick anyone as they arrive" rule, so people who arrive early still end up with more friends.

This project's simplified model illustrating the "friendship paradox" laid out in Scott L. Feld (1991), "Why your friends have more friends than you do", American Journal of Sociology 96(6). It does not reproduce the paper's numbers. The network rule mixes preferential attachment (the idea behind Barabási and Albert's rule) with uniform choice.
